questions.prompt: Match each report format to what it actually does.
right: Groups by rows and by columns at once, summarizing in the cells where they intersect
A flat list of records with no grouping and no subtotals
Puts up to five report blocks side by side, lined up on a shared grouping field
Groups rows into up to three levels, with subtotals and a grand total
questions.explain: Tabular is a flat list with no grouping at all. Summary groups rows, up to three levels, with subtotals and a grand total. Matrix groups by both rows and columns and summarizes in each cell where they cross. Joined lines up to five blocks side by side on a shared grouping field, which is a different mechanism from either.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to explain joined reports before building one. Select every statement below that's actually true about them, per this course.
options: Each block in a joined report can have its own report type and its own filters
Blocks are lined up on a shared grouping field that must exist in every block
A joined report behaves like a single SQL JOIN, producing one combined row per matching key across all blocks
In most orgs, a joined report cannot be used as a normal dashboard source
A row can show a value in one block and nothing in another block, such as a hot account with no open cases
questions.explain: Each block really is its own mini report, with its own type and filters, lined up with the others on a shared grouping field. Most orgs block joined reports from normal dashboard use. And because each block runs its own query, a row can legitimately have data in one block and nothing in another. The one false statement is the SQL JOIN comparison: a joined report is closer to running separate queries and placing their outputs side by side than to a true SQL join producing one combined row set.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ____ is the template that decides which objects and fields a report can see — pick it before anything else, because you generally cannot swap it later without rebuilding the report.
questions.explain: The report type is the pre-built join that decides which objects and fields are available in the Fields pane. Picking it first matters because changing it later usually means rebuilding the report, not just adjusting a setting.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants a report listing every account that has never had an opportunity. The report is currently built on the standard 'Accounts' report type, which has no cross-filter option exposing Opportunity in the Filters tab. What is the most likely reason, and what should change?
options: The report type doesn't expose a relationship to Opportunity at all — switch to a report type built around Accounts and Opportunities together, so a cross filter to Opportunities becomes available
Add filter logic with NOT, since filter logic can simulate a missing-relationship search without changing the report type
Switch the format from tabular to matrix, since only matrix reports can test for the absence of related records
Add a bucket column on Opportunity Amount and bucket the missing values into "None"
questions.explain: A cross filter's available secondary objects depend entirely on what the report type exposes. If Opportunity isn't reachable from the Accounts report type, no amount of filter logic, format switching, or bucketing will create that relationship — only choosing a report type that actually includes it will.

questions.prompt: A cross filter is written as "Show Me Accounts without Opportunities where Stage equals Closed Won." Which statement correctly describes which accounts this returns?
options: Accounts that have no Closed Won opportunity, though they may still have open or other-stage opportunities
Accounts that have no opportunities of any kind, because the sub-filter widens WITHOUT to cover every stage instead of narrowing it
Accounts that have at least one Closed Won opportunity
Accounts that have no opportunities of any kind, except accounts with at least one open opportunity
Accounts whose only opportunities are in the Closed Won stage
Accounts that have more open opportunities than Closed Won opportunities
questions.explain: WITHOUT keeps parent records that have no related record matching the condition given. A sub-filter narrows which related records count — it does not widen WITHOUT into "no opportunities of any kind." So this cross filter returns accounts with no Closed Won opportunity specifically; those accounts may well have open or lost opportunities sitting on them, which is exactly the trap this course warns about.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the right instinct — that a sub-filter changes what WITHOUT tests — but gets the direction backwards. A sub-filter narrows the related records WITHOUT checks against (here, just Closed Won ones), it doesn't widen the condition to mean every stage. Reading the cross filter as a sentence, exactly as the lesson recommends, is the fastest way to catch this.

questions.prompt: A report has three field filters. Select every true statement about how filter logic actually behaves, per this course.
options: With no filter logic set, the three filters combine as 1 AND 2 AND 3
Filter logic can reference the Show Me scope and date filter by number, the same as field filters
Deleting one of the three filters renumbers the remaining ones, so the filter logic expression should be rechecked
Writing 1 OR 2 AND 3 with no parentheses is something this course says to rely on with confidence, since there is no ambiguity to worry about
Cross filters are combined into the report with AND and cannot be placed inside a filter-logic OR expression
questions.explain: By default every field filter combines with AND. Deleting a filter renumbers the rest, so a saved filter-logic string can silently point at the wrong condition afterward. Cross filters sit outside the numbered expression entirely and are always ANDed on top. The false statements are: the Show Me scope and date filter are standard filters that sit outside the numbered field-filter expression, not inside it; and the course explicitly warns to add parentheses when mixing AND and OR rather than trusting unparenthesized precedence.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ____ column groups the values of another field into bands you define, such as Small/Medium/Large deal size — it lives only inside the one report where you build it and cannot be queried with SOQL.
questions.explain: A bucket column is the click-built, report-only equivalent of a CASE expression. It exists only inside the report where it was created, which is exactly why the same categories needed across many dashboards call for a formula field instead.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating a bucket column in the Report Builder in the correct order.
items: Open the source column's dropdown menu and choose Bucket this Column
Name the bucket field and name each bucket
Assign ranges for a number field, or select which values belong in each bucket for a picklist or text field
Apply the bucket, then add it as a grouping to summarize the report by it
questions.explain: Bucketing starts from the source column's own menu, where you name the new field and its buckets, then define what falls into each one — ranges for numbers, selected values for picklists or text — and only once that's applied does the bucket behave like any other column you can group and chart by.

questions.prompt: A report needs weighted pipeline: each opportunity's Amount multiplied by its Probability, then summed by Owner. A colleague instead builds a summary formula that multiplies Sum of Amount by Sum of Probability for each owner's group. What's wrong with the colleague's approach, and what should replace it?
options: Multiplying the already-summed Amount by the already-summed Probability is a different, wrong calculation — the weighting has to happen on each row first, with a row-level formula, before the result is summed by owner
Summary formulas can't reference the Probability field at all, so the fix is to ask an admin for a formula field on the Opportunity object instead
Nothing is wrong — Sum of Amount multiplied by Sum of Probability for a group always equals the sum of each row's Amount times Probability
The formula should use PARENTGROUPVAL on Amount instead of SUM, since PARENTGROUPVAL is the only function that multiplies two summarized fields correctly
questions.explain: The report engine evaluates row-level formulas first, then filters and groups, then runs summary formulas on the already-aggregated totals. Multiplying Amount by Probability has to happen per row, before grouping, or the math is simply wrong — multiplying two sums together is not the same number as summing each row's own product.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a summary formula that needs the grand total of a summarized field, to compute each group's percent of the total, uses ____(field:SUM, GRAND_SUMMARY).
questions.explain: PARENTGROUPVAL fetches a summarized value from a higher grouping level, including the grand total via GRAND_SUMMARY, which is exactly what a share-of-total formula divides into.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the formula functions available in Salesforce reports, per this course.
options: PARENTGROUPVAL and PREVGROUPVAL are only available in summary formulas, since they depend on the report's grouping structure
Row-level formulas generally offer a broader set of text and date functions than summary formulas do
IF(test, if_true, if_false) is the formula-editor equivalent of a T-SQL CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END
Dividing by a RowCount of zero always returns zero instead of an error, so no defensive formula logic is ever needed
BLANKVALUE(field, 0) is the formula-editor equivalent of T-SQL's ISNULL(x, 0)
questions.explain: Group-aware functions only make sense where a grouping exists, so they're summary-only. Row-level formulas carry the richer text and date toolkit. IF nests the same way nested CASE WHEN does, and BLANKVALUE substitutes a default for a blank the same way ISNULL does. The false statement is the zero-division claim: the course is explicit that dividing by zero errors out or returns blank, which is exactly why ratios need a guard such as an IF on the denominator.

questions.prompt: On a tabular report with no row limit set, the Add Chart button is greyed out. Why, and what is the most direct fix?
options: A chart needs grouped, summarized data to plot, and a plain tabular report has neither — add a grouping (making it a summary or matrix report) or set a row limit
Charts only work on report types that include Opportunities, so switch the report type
The report needs a summary formula added before any chart option becomes available
Add Chart is disabled on every tabular report permanently, with no workaround possible
questions.explain: A chart's axes come from a grouping and a summarized value. A tabular report has neither by default, so there's nothing to plot — add a grouping to turn it into a summary or matrix report, or set a row limit, which is the one exception the lesson calls out for tabular reports feeding a chart.

questions.prompt: Match each chart type to the question it's best suited to answer.
right: Plots two numeric measures per group to spot clusters and outliers
Shows how records narrow through ordered stages, such as a pipeline from Prospecting to Closed Won
Shows change over time, grouped by a date at a sensible granularity such as month
Shows parts of a whole, and reads clearly only with a handful of slices
questions.explain: Funnel charts follow a picklist's natural order to show stage-by-stage drop-off. Donuts show a few parts of a whole and get unreadable with many slices. Lines show change over time at a chosen date granularity. Scatter plots two measures against each other to spot clusters and outliers.

questions.prompt: A dashboard is built with a fixed running user who is a VP with broad visibility into every opportunity, including some marked private. The dashboard is then shared with the entire sales team. What is the actual risk, and how does switching to a dynamic dashboard address it?
options: Every viewer currently sees the VP's full access, including private records they shouldn't see; a dynamic dashboard makes each viewer's own access the running context, so they only see what their own role and sharing rules allow
There is no real risk, because dashboard filters already restrict each viewer to their own records regardless of the running user
The risk is that the dashboard will fail to refresh on a schedule; switching to dynamic dashboards fixes scheduled refreshes for a broad audience
The risk is that the VP's dashboard will show stale data; a dynamic dashboard always shows live, unrefreshed data instead
questions.explain: A fixed running user means every viewer sees exactly what that user is allowed to see, not their own access — which is powerful but risky when the running user can see more than some viewers should. A dynamic dashboard makes the logged-in viewer the running user, so each person's own sharing rules govern what they see.

questions.prompt: A dashboard filter isn't behaving the way a colleague expects. Select every true statement below about how dashboard filters actually work.
options: A dashboard filter only narrows a widget whose source report includes the filtered field, typically through its report type
A dashboard filter edits the underlying source reports, so the filter condition gets saved into every report it touches
Lightning dashboards generally allow only a small number of filters per dashboard, commonly three
A dashboard filter behaves like an extra WHERE condition appended on top of each widget's own report filters
Legacy table components are documented as compatible with dashboard filters in every case, the same as Lightning tables
questions.explain: A dashboard filter only reaches a widget whose source report actually contains the filtered field, caps out around three per dashboard in most orgs, and layers on top of each report's own filters like an extra WHERE condition. It changes what's displayed, not what's stored, so it never edits the source reports. And legacy table components are specifically called out as incompatible with dashboard filters, unlike Lightning tables.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every dashboard has a ____ user, and that user's own record access decides what data the dashboard actually shows to every viewer — unless the dashboard is dynamic.
questions.explain: The running user is the access context a dashboard's data is drawn under. A fixed running user means everyone sees what that one user can see; a dynamic dashboard replaces that fixed user with each viewer's own identity.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of adding a dashboard filter in the Lightning Dashboard Builder in the correct order.
items: Click the + Filter button in the dashboard toolbar
Pick the field to filter on, such as Type or Account Name
Give the filter a display name viewers will understand
Set the values or ranges viewers can choose from
questions.explain: The filter builder opens from + Filter, then asks for the field, a viewer-facing display name, and the values or ranges on offer, and none of it takes effect for viewers until the dashboard is saved.

questions.prompt: Match each dashboard widget type to what it actually shows.
right: Shows stage-by-stage drop-off, such as the opportunity pipeline from Prospecting to Closed Won
Shows a Lightning table of up to 10 columns and 200 rows, drawn from the report type
Shows one number against a range, useful against a target
Shows one big number, such as total pipeline
questions.explain: Metric is a single headline number. Gauge places one number against a range toward a target. Table is a Lightning table capped at 10 columns and 200 rows. Funnel shows stage-by-stage drop-off following the picklist's order.

questions.prompt: A sales team wins most of its small deals this quarter but loses most of its large deals. Which statement correctly describes how its count-based win rate and value-based win rate would differ?
options: Count-based win rate would look strong, while value-based win rate would look weak, because losing the large deals removes a disproportionate share of the dollar total
Value-based win rate would look strong while count-based win rate would look weak, because large deals count for more in both measures
The two measures would always be identical in this scenario, since win rate is calculated the exact same way no matter how large or small any individual deal happens to be or how many deals there are
Count-based win rate cannot be calculated unless a Loss Reason field exists on the Opportunity object
Value-based win rate requires Campaign Influence to be enabled before it can be calculated
Both measures would look weak, because losing even one large deal drives every win-rate calculation to zero
questions.explain: Count-based win rate asks what share of deals were won — since most deals are small and most of those were won, that number stays strong. Value-based win rate asks what share of dollars were won, and the lost large deals pull a disproportionate amount of money out of that total, so it looks weak. A team can win most of its deals and lose most of its revenue, which is exactly why this course recommends showing both.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct shape of the answer — the two measures diverge — but swaps which one is strong and which is weak. It's count-based that stays strong here, driven by the many small wins; value-based is the one dragged down by the lost large deals, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on an opportunity, the Forecast Category is usually set automatically from the ____, and its standard values form a ladder from Closed up through Commit and Best Case to Pipeline.
questions.explain: Forecast Category is driven by Stage in most orgs, which is what lets a report grouped by Forecast Category read as a ladder: Closed is the floor, Closed plus Commit is the call, and adding Best Case is the stretch.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about pipeline coverage and forecast reporting, per this course.
options: Pipeline coverage is open pipeline divided by the remaining target, and a common rule of thumb is around three times coverage
A standard Opportunity report can natively divide pipeline by quota, because quota is stored as a field on every Opportunity record
The Forecasts page is optimized for a quick "what is my number" roll-up, while a report is better for slicing by product, source, or stage
Forecast accuracy compares what was predicted at the start of a period with what actually closed, and a standard report alone shows only today's data, not last month's prediction
Forecast Category can never be edited directly by a rep — it only ever reflects the Stage automatically
questions.explain: Coverage is open pipeline over the remaining target, commonly judged against roughly three-times coverage. The Forecasts page suits the weekly roll-up, while reports suit slicing. And accuracy needs a captured prediction to compare against, which a standard report showing only today's data can't supply on its own. The false statements: quota lives with the forecasting feature, not as a field on Opportunity, so a standard report can't divide by it directly; and some orgs do let reps override Forecast Category by hand rather than it always following Stage automatically.

questions.prompt: A marketing report shows that leads created this month have only a 2% conversion rate, versus 35% for leads created a year ago, and leadership concludes this month's leads are much worse quality. What is the more likely explanation, per this course's cohort trap?
options: This month's leads haven't had time to convert yet — comparing a nearly-new cohort to a fully matured one makes the newer leads look worse than they actually are
The Leads report type stopped tracking the Converted checkbox for records created this month
Lead Source values were renamed this month, so the filter silently excludes this month's converted leads
Leads created this month are duplicates that were never actually worked by sales
questions.explain: Comparing a cohort that's only days old against one that's had a full year to convert will always make the newer cohort look worse, regardless of actual lead quality. The fix is to either report on a closed period old enough that every lead has had time to convert, or to read the rate as a cohort trend that's expected to keep climbing.

questions.prompt: Select every service metric below that, per this course, generally needs more than a standard Case report to measure natively.
options: Customer satisfaction (CSAT or NPS)
Case volume by Case Origin
First response time and SLA compliance
Backlog of open cases by Priority
First contact resolution
questions.explain: CSAT/NPS comes from surveys, first response time and SLA compliance depend on Entitlements and Milestones or custom timestamps, and first contact resolution usually needs a custom checkbox or calculated field — none of these exist out of the box. Case volume by Origin and backlog by Priority are both plain groupings on standard Case fields, so they need nothing extra.

questions.prompt: A campaign's Actual Cost is $8,000 and the Total Value Won Opportunities linked to it is $28,000. Using this course's ROI formula, what is the campaign's ROI?
options: 20,000, because ROI is simply revenue minus cost with no division
questions.explain: ROI is (value won minus actual cost) divided by actual cost: (28,000 − 8,000) ÷ 8,000 = 20,000 ÷ 8,000 = 2.5, or 250%. The profit is divided by the cost, not left as a raw dollar figure, which is what turns it into a comparable rate across campaigns of different sizes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the standard Salesforce attribution model credits only one campaign per opportunity, through that opportunity's ____ field, so earlier and later marketing touches get no credit unless Campaign Influence is enabled.
questions.explain: An opportunity's roll-up value flows back to whichever campaign is recorded in its Primary Campaign Source field. Only one campaign can hold that credit at a time, which is the single-source limitation Campaign Influence is designed to get around.

questions.prompt: A VP wants one dashboard combining Salesforce pipeline with monthly revenue pulled from the company's ERP system, refreshed weekly. Which of this course's five deciding questions does this request fail natively, and what does that imply?
options: It needs data from outside Salesforce, which cannot be blended into a native report — this points toward CRM Analytics, Tableau, or a warehouse-and-BI approach instead of a standard dashboard
It needs more than three grouping levels, which a summary report cannot provide, so the fix is to switch to a matrix report
It needs more than three cross filters, which no report format supports, so the fix is a joined report instead
It needs a dynamic dashboard, since only dynamic dashboards can refresh on a weekly schedule
questions.explain: ERP revenue lives outside Salesforce, and native reports can only use data that already lives in Salesforce. That's the question about outside data specifically, and it's the signal to look at CRM Analytics, Tableau, or a warehouse-and-BI approach rather than trying to force it into a standard dashboard.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder assumes native reporting has no real limits. Select every true statement below about where it actually runs out, per this course.
options: Every report is built on a report type, a fixed, predefined path through related objects, not an arbitrary join on any matching key
A standard report shows records as they are right now; reconstructing history that was never captured requires something set up in advance, such as reporting snapshots
Reporting snapshots can retroactively build history for any period before the snapshot was created
Report formulas can compute across data already in the report, but not across unrelated objects or outside systems such as an ERP or a spreadsheet
Because reports query live data, very large objects or complex cross filters can be slow or time out, a limit no amount of report redesign fully removes
questions.explain: Report types fix the path through related objects, reports show only the present unless history was deliberately captured, formulas can't reach outside the report's own data, and scale genuinely limits performance regardless of design. The false statement is about snapshots: they only start capturing from the day they're set up, so they can never build history for a period before that — neither snapshots nor any other native feature can travel back and create history nobody recorded.

questions.prompt: Put these five steps of the capstone's repeatable report-building plan in the correct order.
items: Write the question the report must answer
Choose the report type that already has the fields the question needs
Build the report, adding filters, grouping, and any formula the question requires
Choose a chart type that fits the comparison, then format it
Assemble the dashboard, adding components and dashboard filters, and reconcile every number
questions.explain: The plan always starts from the business question, then picks the report type that can actually answer it, builds the report itself, picks a chart that fits the comparison, and only then assembles and reconciles the dashboard — doing these out of order, such as picking a chart before the report exists, leaves nothing to format.

questions.prompt: A Workload by Owner bar chart, built from open Cases grouped by Case Owner, shows a bar labeled "Tier 1" that is larger than every individual agent's bar. What does that bar most likely represent, and how should it be presented to the VP?
options: Cases still sitting in the Tier 1 queue, not yet assigned to a person — label it clearly as a queue, separate from the agent bars, so it isn't mistaken for one overloaded agent
A data error, since Case Owner should only ever be an individual user, so the chart needs to be rebuilt from a different report type
The single top-performing agent on the Tier 1 support team, who happens to be named "Tier 1" in the org's user records
The total of every agent's cases added together, which should be removed from the chart to avoid double counting
questions.explain: Case Owner can be a queue as well as a person, and cases waiting in a queue haven't been assigned to any individual agent yet. The chart title should call that bar out explicitly as a queue, not an agent, so the VP doesn't read it as one person carrying an unreasonable workload.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: with a $6.0M quota and $3.9M already Closed Won this quarter, the remaining gap is $2.1M; if open pipeline closing this quarter is $4.2M, the coverage is $4.2M divided by $2.1M, or ____x.
questions.explain: The remaining gap is $6.0M minus $3.9M, or $2.1M. Dividing the $4.2M of open pipeline closing this quarter by that $2.1M gap gives exactly 2.0x coverage of what's still needed to hit quota.
